description:
What happened the last times a US airport looked like this: precedent days for a bad day of
cancellations, precedent diversions for a destination, or one aircraft's day, from the US DOT
on-time record.

Use it when someone is deciding or explaining, and history would help: whether to cancel or hold,
how long a bad day took to clear last time, where flights for an airport diverted and whether they
got there, why a passenger's day went the way it did. It gives context and dated examples, not the
live picture.

`kind="airport_days"`: `airport` is the DEPARTURE airport. With `like_date` (YYYY-MM-DD) it returns
`the_day` (scheduled, cancelled, the coded causes, the carriers, and the disruption it was part of)
and the airport's other disruptions as `precedents`, matched on the share cancelled and the coded
cause, always with one of a different cause for contrast. Without `like_date` it lists the largest.
A disruption is this tool's own term: it starts on a day when `min_share` (default 0.15) or more of
scheduled departures were cancelled after a day under it, and ends on the first later day under
0.05. Each has `days_to_recover` and `following_days` (the share cancelled on each day after).

`kind="diversions"`: `airport` is the DESTINATION. `months` is a list of month numbers to read
across every year held, e.g. [6, 7, 8]; omit it for all months. It returns how often flights
diverted, `alternates` (where they landed, whether they then reached the destination and how late),
the days it clustered on with some of the flights as rows, and one aircraft's later departures that
day as a knock-on example.

`kind="aircraft_day"`: one aircraft's flights on one LOCAL date, in order: give `like_date` and
either `registration` (N27511) or `flight`, a flight it flew that day in the two-character form
(UA2815, the iata_form from parse_flight_identifier; not UAL2815). No `airport`. Each leg has its
scheduled and actual times, minutes late, any cancellation or diversion, the carrier's cause minutes,
and `inbound_arrived_after_scheduled_departure_min`: above zero, the aircraft landed after this
flight was due to leave. `annotation.where_delay_entered` names the first late leg. Use it to see
whether a delay was inherited from the aircraft's earlier flying; it never says why the first delay
happened.

`carrier` (two-character reporting carrier code, e.g. DL) narrows the first two kinds. `limit` is the number
of precedents (1 to 8, default 3).


NOT LIVE AND NOT A FORECAST: a record of July 2024 to August 2026, published two to three months in arrears by the US DOT Bureau of Transportation Statistics; not endorsed by BTS or DOT. Say so when you quote it, and give the window. SCOPE: US domestic flights of the carriers that report on-time data to DOT (12 to 15 large carriers), so NO count is an airport's total traffic. Airports are three-letter codes as BTS gives them (ATL, JFK, ORD); resolve a name with resolve_airport first. Times are local to the airport where each event happened. The cause of a cancellation is the carrier's own code (carrier, weather, air traffic system, security): nobody independent assigned it, and `cause_share` says how much of the day the leading code covers. A diversion carries NO reason in this source: you can say where a flight landed and how late it arrived, never why. Reading the answer: `status` is resolved, none_found (nothing matched; with a note), not_covered (the date is outside the window -- never evidence that nothing happened), unresolved (the input could not be used; the note says why) or unavailable. Read `baseline` first, then `precedents`, then `annotation`; copy `not_to_be_read_as` rather than soften it. `annotation.pattern` is a count over one airport and one window: quote it as a count, with the window, never as a rule. No precedent is an answer: if nothing in the window resembles the day, say so.
name: disruption_precedents
title: Disruption precedents
